During the home interview on 10/05/2026, Sofía’s mother reported that Sofía lives with her, her 6-year-old brother Diego and her maternal grandmother. Her mother works from 8:00 a.m. to 5:00 p.m., and her grandmother cares for the children from 3:00 to 5:30 p.m. Her mother completed the interview in English and reported that Sofía’s grandmother speaks only Spanish and that her father lives in another state and has no regular contact. When asked what she wanted from treatment, her mother said she wanted Sofía to stop hurting Diego, calm down without breaking things and go to school without a fight. She also wants Sofía to have at least 1 friend and to shower on her own.

According to the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation, Sofía’s pediatrician and primary care physician, Ramón Ejemplar, M.D., referred her because of aggression at home and school, explosive outbursts, leaving the classroom, refusing to go to school and a lack of friendships. Marta Supuesta, Ph.D., a licensed psychologist, evaluated Sofía on 07/15/2026 and 07/22/2026. In her report signed 07/30/2026, Dr. Supuesta diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder (F84.0), without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language; and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation (F90.2). Dr. Supuesta recommended ABA at home and in the community with parent training, continued school speech-language services for pragmatics, a social skills group, continued medication management and coordination with the school team. Dr. Ejemplar signed the physician’s order for behavior analysis services on 08/04/2026. According to the evaluation, Sofía’s psychiatrist, Iván Hipotético, M.D., prescribed methylphenidate extended release 18 mg every morning beginning in March 2026. Her mother reported psychiatry follow-up every 6 weeks and said that Sofía focuses better in the morning but that afternoon outbursts are “worse than before.”

Sofía’s mother reported that Sofía was born at 39 weeks without complications, met her early developmental milestones on time and spoke in sentences by age 2. Her mother recalled that teachers first raised concerns in kindergarten about outbursts and playing alone. Although Sofía uses complete sentences, her current IEP describes difficulty taking turns in conversation, staying on topic and understanding nonliteral language. Dr. Supuesta also noted that Sofía talks at length about trains without asking questions in return and does not clarify what she means when someone misunderstands her.

Her mother reported that Sofía attends 4th grade at Ejemplo Elementary School from 8:30 a.m. to 3:00 p.m. in a general education classroom with ESE support. The IEP in effect from 04/17/2026 to 04/16/2027 identifies Autism Spectrum Disorder as her primary exceptionality and Other Health Impairment (ADHD) as secondary. The IEP describes grade-level reading with strong decoding and vocabulary, but places math about 1 year below grade level and notes that Sofía does not finish independent work. Through the IEP, Sofía receives 300 minutes per week of specialized instruction through support facilitation in general education, 60 minutes per week of speech-language therapy for pragmatic language and 30 minutes per week of school counseling. The IEP includes a visual schedule, a break card, advance warning before transitions, seating away from the door, extended time on assignments and access to headphones in the cafeteria. Its goals address using the break card instead of leaving class, taking conversational turns on a peer’s topic and using a calming strategy when frustrated. The IEP does not include behavior analysis services; her mother reported on 10/28/2026 that the school-based Functional Behavior Assessment requested on 04/17/2026 was still pending. Her mother also reported that Sofía received 6 months of school counseling in 2024, that she saw no change during that period and that Sofía has never received ABA.

At home, Sofía’s mother described hitting, kicking and pushing Diego over the tablet or TV remote, yelling insults and threats after school or at bedtime, tearing homework and biting her hand or wrist when frustrated. On school mornings, her mother reported that Sofía sometimes locks herself in the bathroom or refuses to board the bus; her mother has arrived late to work or her grandmother has kept Sofía home. At school, the IEP describes leaving class during writing or group work and pushing or kicking peers at lunch and recess. In daily care, her mother reported that Sofía can dress herself but needs repeated reminders to shower and does not wash her hair independently. In the community, her mother reported that Sofía runs across streets without looking when excited and cannot order food or pay at a store.

Her mother described Sofía as affectionate with her grandmother and said she helps feed the family dog, enjoys train books and draws maps. She also reported that Sofía plays alone on her tablet and has no friends at school or in the neighborhood. Dr. Supuesta documented that Sofía misreads peers’ teasing as aggression and covers her ears and leaves the room in the cafeteria and during assemblies. Her mother described similar difficulty continuing an outing when the route home changes: Sofía screams and refuses to get out of the car. At home, her mother said that even a late dinner disrupts the evening routine, and she reported that she has begun avoiding family outings.

sections.text:
Daniela Muestra, M.S., BCBA, reviewed the Comprehensive Diagnostic Evaluation signed on 07/30/2026 by Marta Supuesta, Ph.D., licensed psychologist, and the 04/17/2026 IEP from Ejemplo Elementary School. Dr. Supuesta diagnosed Autism Spectrum Disorder (F84.0), without accompanying intellectual impairment, with accompanying language impairment in pragmatic language [MISSING: severity level, not in the CDE]; and Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder, combined presentation (F90.2). On 10/05/2026, the BCBA interviewed Sofía’s mother, who completed the Vineland-3 Comprehensive Parent/Caregiver Interview Form, the BASC-3 Parenting Relationship Questionnaire (PRQ), Child/Adolescent form, the FAST, the MAS and the caregiver FBA interview. The BCBA also drew on the 10/28/2026 follow-up interview and her direct observations at home on 10/07/2026 and 10/14/2026 and at the public library and neighborhood park on 10/10/2026. Together, these findings identify needs in self-care and daily living, communication, coping with change and demands, safety, and participation with peers and in the community.

On the Vineland-3, Sofía’s Adaptive Behavior Composite of 74 was Moderately Low, at the 4th percentile: about 4 in 100 children her age would score this low or lower in everyday independence. Daily Living Skills (72, 3rd percentile, Moderately Low) reflected the help her mother described with bathing and purchases; Community, with a v-scale score of 8 (Low), was the weakest daily living subdomain. Communication (81, 10th percentile, Moderately Low) showed difficulty beyond speaking in sentences, a relative strength reflected in her Adequate Expressive v-scale score of 13. Socialization (66, 1st percentile, Low) was her greatest domain weakness. Within it, Coping (v-scale score 5, Low) and Interpersonal Relationships (7, Low) reflect her mother’s account of how hard it is for Sofía to manage a changed routine or make a friend. Motor Skills (88, 21st percentile, Adequate) were a relative strength. On the Maladaptive Behavior domain, her mother’s ratings placed Internalizing at 19 (Elevated), while Externalizing and the Maladaptive Behavior Index were both 22 (Clinically Significant), consistent with her report that hitting, threats and damage to belongings disrupt family routines.

In self-care and daily living, Sofía’s mother reported that Sofía dresses herself but does not wash her hair independently. During the evening observation on 10/14/2026, the BCBA counted 14 verbal prompts over 38 minutes before Sofía entered the shower; even then, she did not wash her hair. Her mother’s goal is for Sofía to shower on her own. She needs to learn both to start the routine with less adult direction and to complete it, including washing her hair.

In communication, Dr. Supuesta found that Sofía does not ask questions in return or clarify a misunderstanding, and the IEP describes difficulty taking turns and understanding nonliteral language. At home on 10/07/2026, the BCBA listened as Sofía spoke about train schedules for 11 minutes without responding to 2 attempts to change the subject. Sofía can explain a familiar subject at length; what she needs to learn is to notice and respond to another person’s contribution so that both can take part.

Difficulty coping with change and demands costs Sofía instructional time. For Leaving the area and school refusal, the IEP documented departures from class 2 to 4 times per week, usually during writing or group work. Dr. Supuesta saw Sofía leave a group activity twice during the summer program on 07/22/2026; she was found in the hallway. Her mother reported refusal on 6 of 20 school days in October [CHECK: confirm the attendance period; the interview documenting this October total is dated 10/05/2026]. Her mother described arriving late to work or having Sofía stay home with her grandmother. Her MAS ratings ranked escape highest (5.0), supporting the hypothesis that leaving or refusing school allows Sofía to avoid academic or social demands. At home, her mother also identified Verbal outbursts and Property destruction as barriers to completing homework. ABA will address asking for a break or help, returning to unfinished work and managing changes without breaking things, in keeping with her mother’s priorities for homework and school mornings.

Physical aggression places Diego and other children at risk. Sofía’s mother reported that Diego had a bruise on his upper arm, and the IEP documented pushing or kicking peers about 2 times per week, mostly at lunch and recess. The BCBA recorded 6 episodes in 6 hours across home and community observations, including pushing Diego to the floor and kicking his leg after he picked up her train book. Her mother endorsed 4 of 4 FAST escape items; her MAS ratings favored escape (4.5) over access to preferred items (3.8), supporting the BCBA’s primary escape and secondary preferred-item hypotheses. Safety concerns also include Hand biting (self-injury) and leaving an adult’s side: on 10/10/2026, the BCBA saw Sofía pull free of her mother’s hand and run across the street without looking. Sofía needs to manage demands and conflicts over belongings without hurting herself or others and to cross streets safely with an adult.

In peer and community participation, the BCBA saw 2 girls invite Sofía to play tag at the park on 10/10/2026. Sofía recited the bus schedule; the girls walked away, and she played alone. Her mother reported no friendships at school or in the neighborhood and said that she has begun avoiding outings. She also reported that Sofía cannot order food or pay at a store and becomes upset when a cashier speaks to her. To participate beyond familiar family routines, Sofía needs to learn to respond to invitations, join play and complete purchases.

The BCBA’s observations showed what happened immediately after demands and transitions. At home on 10/07/2026, neither homework attempt was completed; after Sofía tore her worksheet and screamed, her grandmother gave her the tablet, and she calmed within 2 minutes. At the library on 10/10/2026, screaming when it was time to leave lasted 9 minutes, until a staff member asked her mother to take her outside. At home on 10/14/2026, even a 10-minute delay in dinner preceded screaming and hitting. School evidence comes from the IEP and Dr. Supuesta’s observation; district approval for the BCBA to observe was pending.

These findings establish the medical necessity of individualized ABA at home, where demands interrupt hygiene and homework and Diego is at risk, and in the community, where street crossings, purchases and peer play require skills Sofía does not yet use independently. Teaching will match skills to what the behaviors help Sofía obtain or avoid. Her mother’s At-Risk BASC-3 PRQ scores for Parenting Confidence (T-score 34), Discipline Practices (36) and Relational Frustration (68), together with her report of exhaustion, support training her mother and grandmother in responses they can use during these routines. Coordination with the school and psychiatrist will complement specialized instruction, pragmatic language therapy, school counseling and medication management by addressing how Sofía uses skills outside school. The BCBA will judge progress by direct data on target behaviors, prompts needed for self-care, independent responses and participation in family and community activities, together with Vineland-3 and BASC-3 PRQ results at reassessment.

On the way to the park on 10/10/2026, the BCBA saw Sofía pull her wrist free of her mother’s hand before running across the street without looking. Her mother reported that Sofía runs across without looking when excited and that she holds Sofía’s wrist in parking lots. Other signs depend on the setting: Dr. Marta Supuesta documented covering her ears and leaving noisy settings, while her mother described crying, locking herself in the bathroom or refusing to board the bus on school mornings. During the evening observation on 10/14/2026, the BCBA heard Sofía scream “everything is ruined” when dinner was late, then saw her kick over a chair and hit her mother’s arm. Separately, her mother reported that Sofía banged her head against the bedroom wall during an outburst on 09/14/2026. Her grandmother took her to urgent care, where a cut above her eyebrow was closed with skin glue, according to her mother; the urgent care record was unavailable.
